category: Backend stack decisions and scientific Python tooling (for ADRs)
summary: Research date 2026-08-22. Database: PostgreSQL 18.6 is the current stable line (19 is at Beta 3); PostGIS 3.6.1 is current stable (3.7.0beta2 adds PG19). TimescaleDB 2.29.2 supports PG 16-18, but every feature that matters for an observation store (columnstore/compression, continuous aggregates, retention policies, background jobs) is Timescale/Tiger License (TSL) only; the Apache-2 edition is essentially hypertable chunking. For ~thousands of observation series (e.g. 5,000 series x 96 obs/day ~ 175M rows/yr, INFERENCE) plain declarative partitioning (monthly RANGE on observed_at) managed by pg_partman 5.5.0's background worker is sufficient and keeps hosting options open; PostgreSQL docs say the planner handles 'up to a few thousand partitions fairly well' when pruning applies. Python: FastAPI 0.141.1 now requires Pydantic v2 (v1 dropped in 0.126, pydantic.v1 shim dropped in 0.128); Pydantic 2.13.4; SQLAlchemy 2.0.52 async via asyncpg 0.31.0 or psycopg 3.3.4 (psycopg is the one DBAPI that serves both create_engine and create_async_engine from the same URL); Alembic 1.19.1 with the `-t async` template; GeoAlchemy2 0.20.0 with Alembic helpers. Scientific wheels (rasterio 1.5.1, rioxarray 0.23.0, zarr 3.3.0, VirtualiZarr 2.7.3, Icechunk 2.1.2) require Python >=3.12, so the project floor is Python 3.12. Jobs with Postgres as the only infrastructure: recommend Procrastinate 3.9.0 (psycopg3, async-native, LISTEN/NOTIFY + SELECT FOR UPDATE, retry strategies with linear/exponential wait, DB-coordinated cron so 'deferring only happens once per period, even with multiple workers', `lock` for per-resource serialization, `queueing_lock` for enqueue-time dedupe, heartbeats + get_stalled_jobs). PgQueuer 1.3.2 is the strongest alternative (asyncpg or psycopg, SKIP LOCKED, dedupe_key unique partial index, DatabaseRetryEntrypointExecutor backoff, automatic heartbeat_timeout re-pickup, cron SchedulerManager, Prometheus/tracing/dashboard) but younger. APScheduler 3.11.3 is in-process only (4.0 is alpha: 'do NOT use this release in production'); Celery 5.6.3 has no PostgreSQL broker and beat must be a single instance; Dramatiq 2.2.0 (LGPL) and arq 0.28.0 ('maintained in a limited capacity') need Redis/RabbitMQ; Prefect 3.8.3 and Dagster 1.13.19 (both Apache-2.0) are full orchestration products needing their own server/daemon/DB and are overweight as the job engine for a modular monolith, though Dagster's asset graph is a credible later layer. Object storage: MinIO's GitHub repo is archived (read-only since 2026-04-25, 'THIS REPOSITORY IS NO LONGER MAINTAINED', community edition source-only, last binary release 2025-10-15) - do not adopt. SeaweedFS 4.44 (Apache-2.0, `weed mini` single-node, versioning/lifecycle/tagging/object-lock per its wiki) or Garage v2.3.0 (AGPLv3, no versioning/tagging) for self-hosted/dev; Cloudflare R2 ($0.015/GB-month, zero egress, 10 GB free, but no versioning/tagging) or S3 for production. Use obstore 0.11.1 (Rust object_store, sync+async, S3-compatible endpoints, fsspec adapter, also backs zarr's experimental ObjectStore) as the primary client; boto3 1.43.78 for admin; aioboto3 15.5.0 only if boto3 parity is needed. Science: xarray 2026.7.0; cfgrib 0.9.15.1 + eccodes 2.47.0 (pip wheels bundle eccodeslib since 2.43.0 - no conda required); Herbie 2026.3.0 for HRRR/GFS/GEFS/NBM/RRFS/RTMA/ECMWF from AWS NODD/GCP/Azure/NOMADS; exactextract 0.3.0 (fractional pixel coverage, coverage_weight, min_coverage_frac, weighted_* ops) over rasterstats 0.21.0 for basin-average zonal statistics on 3-km grids against small Cascade basins; pyproj 3.7.2, shapely 2.1.2, GeoPandas 1.1.4; Zarr 3.3.0 (spec v2+v3, sharding; avoid yanked 3.0.0-3.0.7), kerchunk 0.2.10, VirtualiZarr 2.7.3 (alpha), Icechunk 2.1.2; pint 0.25.3 + pint-xarray 0.6.1. Observability: OpenTelemetry Python traces and metrics are Stable, logs still 'Development' (SDK 1.44.0) with instrumentations for fastapi/asgi/sqlalchemy/asyncpg/psycopg/httpx/logging/system-metrics; structlog 26.1.0; prometheus_client 0.26.0 multiprocess mode has real limitations (no Info/Enum, custom collectors don't work) so prefer OTLP metrics or one process per container; Grafana is AGPL-3.0-only. Testing: pytest 9.1.1, pytest-asyncio 1.4.0 (asyncio_mode, asyncio_default_fixture_loop_scope, asyncio_default_test_loop_scope), respx 0.23.1 (httpx>=0.25) vs pytest-httpx 0.36.2 (pins httpx==0.28.*, pytest==9.*), testcontainers 4.15.0 (PostgresContainer accepts a custom image, e.g. a postgis image), schemathesis 4.25.0 (OpenAPI 3.1/3.2, from_asgi for FastAPI), Playwright 1.62.0, hypothesis 6.165.10 (MPL-2.0).

providers.name: PostgreSQL 18 + PostGIS 3.6 (core relational/spatial store)
providers.authority: PostgreSQL Global Development Group; PostGIS Project Steering Committee (OSGeo)

access.mechanism: Self-hosted server software (apt/yum/Docker) or managed PostgreSQL; accessed via libpq-compatible drivers (asyncpg, psycopg 3)
access.auth: SCRAM-SHA-256 (md5 deprecated in PG 18); OAuth 2.0 mechanism new in PG 18
formats: SQL over PostgreSQL wire protocol (protocol 3.2 introduced in PG 18)

providers.cadence: One major release per year (September); quarterly minor releases. PG 18.6 released 2026-08-13; PG 19 Beta 3 released 2026-08-13. PostGIS 3.6.1 released 2025-11-12; 3.7.0beta2 2026-08-10.
providers.spatial_resolution: N/A (PostGIS geometry/geography/raster types at arbitrary precision)
providers.historical_depth: Support window: PG 18 supported until 2030-11-14; PG 17 until 2029-11-08; PG 16 until 2028-11-09; PG 14 ends 2026-11-12.
providers.quality_flags: Production-stable. PG 18 headline features: asynchronous I/O subsystem (io_method worker/io_uring/sync), B-tree skip scan, uuidv7(), virtual generated columns, OLD/NEW in RETURNING, preserved planner statistics across pg_upgrade, page checksums on by default, temporal WITHOUT OVERLAPS constraints.
providers.licensing: PostgreSQL License (permissive; INFERENCE - not read on a fetched page this session). PostGIS is GPLv2+ (INFERENCE - not read this session).
limitations: PostGIS 3.6.1 supports PostgreSQL 12-18; PG 19 support only in the 3.7.0 beta series (3.7.0beta2 supports PG 14-19beta2) - do not plan on PG 19 until PostGIS 3.7.0 final ships.

Declarative partitioning guidance: 'The query planner is generally able to handle partition hierarchies with up to a few thousand partitions fairly well, provided that typical queries allow the query planner to prune all but a small number of partitions'; too many partitions increase planning time and per-session memory because 'each partition requires its metadata to be loaded into the local memory of each session that touches it'.
Partitioned tables need the partition key in PRIMARY KEY/UNIQUE constraints (INFERENCE from general PG behavior; not quoted from the fetched page).
Re-partitioning is slow; the docs advise simulating the workload before committing to a strategy.

evidence.claim: Latest stable PostgreSQL is 18.6 (2026-08-13); PostgreSQL 19 Beta 3 released 2026-08-13
PostGIS 3.6.1 released 2025-11-12 supports 'PostgreSQL 12 - 18'; 3.7.0beta2 (2026-08-10) supports 'PostgreSQL 14 - 19beta2'; 3.6.0 released 2025-09-02

PG 18 released 2025-09-25 with async I/O (io_method worker/io_uring/sync), skip scan, uuidv7(), virtual generated columns, OLD/NEW in RETURNING, statistics preserved by pg_upgrade, checksums default on, OAuth auth, md5 deprecated, protocol 3.2

Planner handles 'up to a few thousand partitions fairly well' with pruning; more remaining partitions after pruning -> longer planning and higher memory; 'Never just assume that more partitions are better than fewer partitions, nor vice-versa'
Volume estimate: 5,000 series x 96 obs/day (15-min) ~ 480k rows/day ~ 175M rows/yr; ~40-50 B/row narrow tuple -> single-digit GB/yr heap - comfortably within plain PG with monthly partitions

providers.relevance_to_cascade_oracle: Primary system of record for stations, series metadata, observations, derived basin aggregates, forecasts, and basin geometries (PostGIS). Adopt PG 18.x now (5-year support to 2030-11) with PostGIS 3.6.1; plan PG 19 only after PostGIS 3.7.0 final. Partition the observation table by month on observed_at (RANGE) with a (series_id, observed_at) composite index; ~12-36 partitions per year-span is far below the 'few thousand' ceiling. uuidv7() is useful for job/event ids; OLD/NEW RETURNING simplifies idempotent upsert auditing.

providers.name: TimescaleDB vs native partitioning + pg_partman (time-series storage decision)
providers.authority: Tiger Data (formerly Timescale) for TimescaleDB; Keith Fiske / pgpartman project for pg_partman

access.mechanism: PostgreSQL extensions (CREATE EXTENSION timescaledb / pg_partman); pg_partman ships a background worker (BGW) for maintenance
access.auth: N/A (database roles; pg_partman 5.5.0 BGW now defaults to a non-superuser role `partman_maintainer`)

providers.cadence: TimescaleDB 2.29.2 released 2026-08-18 (frequent minor releases). pg_partman v5.5.0 released 2026-07-22.
providers.historical_depth: TimescaleDB 2.29.x supports PostgreSQL 16, 17, 18 ('PostgreSQL 15 Support Removed' in 2.29.0). pg_partman requires 'PostgreSQL >= 14'.
providers.quality_flags: Both mature. TimescaleDB 2.28+/2.29 notes: Hypercore engine with faster first()/last() on compressed data, lighter continuous-aggregate refreshes, vectorized CASE on compressed data, DML chunk-exclusion improvements.
providers.licensing: TimescaleDB has two editions: 'Apache 2 Edition' and 'Community Edition' under the Tiger Data License (TSL). Under TSL 'You cannot sell TimescaleDB Community Edition as a service, even if you are the main contributor' but self-hosting for your own product is permitted; 'You can sell TimescaleDB Apache 2 Edition as a service'. pg_partman: repository LICENSE.txt (PostgreSQL-style permissive license, INFERENCE - license text not read).
limitations: Apache-2 TimescaleDB lacks everything that makes it attractive for an observation store: columnstore/hypercore compression (ALTER TABLE ... hypercore, add_columnstore_policy), continuous aggregates (CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW ... continuous aggregate and policies), retention policies (add_retention_policy/remove_retention_policy 'are only available in TimescaleDB Community Edition'), background jobs (add_job/alter_job/delete_job/run_job), and advanced chunk ops (split_chunk/reorder_chunk/move_chunk).

TSL (Community) edition constrains hosting: managed providers must ship it (e.g., AWS RDS does not include TimescaleDB - INFERENCE, not read this session); TSL forbids offering TimescaleDB itself as a service, which is not Cascade Oracle's business model so it is otherwise usable.

pg_partman 5.x supports only native declarative partitioning ('the older trigger-based methods have been deprecated'); v5.5.0 breaking change: pg_partman_bgw.role defaults to partman_maintainer - 'If this parameter had not been explicitly set before, this will cause the BGW to no longer run successfully' without that role; retention schema must be owned by the child-table owner.

Neither native partitioning nor pg_partman provides columnar compression or incremental materialized aggregates; those must be built as ordinary tables refreshed by jobs (Procrastinate periodic tasks) if needed.

evidence.claim: Edition feature split: hypertables/create_hypertable/show_chunks/drop_chunks in both; columnstore/hypercore, continuous aggregates, retention policies, add_job/alter_job, reorder/move/split chunk are Community (TSL) only; 'You cannot sell TimescaleDB Community Edition as a service'
TimescaleDB 2.29.2 released 2026-08-18; supports PostgreSQL 16, 17, 18; 'PostgreSQL 15 Support Removed' in 2.29.0

pg_partman: time- and number-based partition sets, 'PostgreSQL >= 14', 'only built-in, declarative partitioning is supported', includes 'A background worker (BGW) process ... to automatically run partition maintenance without the need of an external scheduler', retention via dropping old partitions

pg_partman latest tag v5.5.0 published 2026-07-22T14:46:50Z; BGW role default changed to partman_maintainer; CVE fixes for SQL injection/privilege escalation; detach-before-drop support; RLS maintenance_role

Recommendation: plain declarative partitioning + pg_partman is sufficient at ~thousands of series; revisit TimescaleDB Community only if storage cost (compression) or dashboard-speed aggregates become the bottleneck

providers.relevance_to_cascade_oracle: ADR recommendation: do NOT adopt TimescaleDB initially. Use native RANGE partitioning (monthly, on observed_at) with pg_partman 5.5.0 BGW for auto-creation and retention; keep a (series_id, observed_at DESC) index per partition, consider BRIN on observed_at for append-only scans. This keeps the schema portable to any PostgreSQL host and avoids TSL. Document the trigger to revisit: >~1B rows or a need for transparent compression/continuous aggregates, at which point TimescaleDB Community (2.29.x on PG 16-18, self-hosted) is license-compatible for a SaaS that is not itself selling TimescaleDB.

providers.name: Procrastinate (recommended Postgres-only job/worker system)

access.mechanism: PyPI package; schema installed into PostgreSQL via `procrastinate schema --apply`; workers run as separate processes sharing the app DB
formats: Python task functions; job rows in PostgreSQL

providers.latency: Near-immediate wake-up via LISTEN/NOTIFY plus periodic polling (fetch_job_polling_interval) for scheduled/locked jobs
providers.temporal_resolution: Cron with 5 columns plus optional 6th seconds column for periodic tasks
providers.historical_depth: Requires Python 3.10+ and PostgreSQL 13+; job history retained until 'Delete finished jobs' maintenance runs
providers.quality_flags: Mature (3.x); MIT; async-native with sync support; Django integration optional; heartbeat-based stalled-job detection
limitations: Stalled-job recovery is not automatic: you must write a periodic task (docs example uses @app.periodic(cron='*/10 * * * *')) that calls JobManager.get_stalled_jobs() and retry_job(); workers heartbeat 'every 10 seconds by default' and jobs are stalled when the worker has no heartbeat 'since the last (by default) 30 seconds'. The nb_seconds parameter is deprecated.
Finished-job cleanup is a manual/periodic concern ('Delete finished jobs' how-to); the jobs table grows otherwise.
A crashed job holding a `lock` blocks 'following jobs with the same lock ... until the interrupted job is either manually set to failed or succeeded' (or retried via the stalled-job task).
No bundled web dashboard or Prometheus exporter (INFERENCE - none seen in fetched docs; PgQueuer has both).

Connectors: PsycopgConnector (async, psycopg 3) and SyncPsycopgConnector; aiopg and psycopg2 connectors are optional extras; sqlalchemy~=2.0 extra exists (deferral-only SQLAlchemy connector - INFERENCE on scope).
At-least-once semantics are implied by the retry/stalled-job design but not stated verbatim on the fetched discussions page.

evidence.claim: Python 3.10+, PostgreSQL 13+, connectors SyncPsycopgConnector/PsycopgConnector, periodic tasks, retries, priorities, locks and queueing locks, Django integration, ASGI-friendly
Latest release tag 3.9.0 published 2026-06-20T23:02:05Z; adds task/worker middleware and Django DB connection management
PyPI 3.9.0: requires_python >=3.10; MIT; deps asgiref, attrs, croniter, packaging, psycopg[pool], python-dateutil, typing-extensions; extras aiopg, psycopg2, django>=2.2, sqlalchemy~=2.0

Uses LISTEN for notifications and 'SELECT FOR UPDATE' locking so 'when a worker starts executing a job, it's the only one'; fetch_job_polling_interval and abort_job_polling_interval; lock = sequential execution per resource

retry=True/int; RetryStrategy(max_attempts, wait, linear_wait, exponential_wait, retry_exceptions); custom BaseRetryStrategy.get_retry_decision -> RetryDecision(retry_in/retry_at, priority, queue, lock)

@app.periodic(cron=...) with 5 or 6 columns; tasks receive `timestamp`; 'the database is responsible for making sure deferring only happens once per period, even with multiple workers'; periodic_id distinguishes multiple schedules

'Trying to defer a task when the queueing_lock is active will result in an AlreadyEnqueued exception, which you can choose to ignore'; queueing_lock allows a single job in todo while multiple may be doing; combine with lock to serialize
Heartbeats every 10 s by default; get_stalled_jobs() fetches doing-jobs of workers without heartbeat for 30 s; retry requires a user-written periodic task calling retry_job(); nb_seconds deprecated

providers.relevance_to_cascade_oracle: ADR recommendation for the modular monolith + workers: Procrastinate 3.9.x. Pattern: one `App` in the monolith package; API process defers jobs inside the same DB transaction as the triggering write (psycopg connector); N worker processes (`procrastinate worker -q ingest,derive,notify`). Idempotency: key ingestion jobs by (source, station_or_basin, window_start) via `queueing_lock` (dedupes pending work) and use `lock` per station/source to serialize fetches; persist with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (series_id, observed_at) DO UPDATE so reruns are safe; periodic tasks get `timestamp` so backfills are deterministic. Retries: RetryStrategy(max_attempts=5, exponential_wait=...) with retry_exceptions limited to transient HTTP/DB errors. Ops: ship a periodic stalled-job retry task and a finished-job deletion task from day one; export worker metrics through OpenTelemetry yourself.

providers.name: PgQueuer (Postgres-only alternative job queue)

access.mechanism: PyPI package; `pgq install` creates tables; PgQueuer.from_asyncpg_pool()/from_asyncpg_connection() and psycopg drivers; in-memory mode for tests
access.rate_limits: Per-entrypoint concurrency_limit enforced in the database
formats: async Python entrypoints; pgqueuer_jobs / pgqueuer_log / pgqueuer_statistics tables

providers.latency: LISTEN/NOTIFY 'wakes workers the moment a job lands' with polling fallback
providers.temporal_resolution: Cron schedules with 5-field (minute) or 6-field (seconds) expressions; execute_after for delayed jobs
providers.quality_flags: Active but younger/smaller project than Procrastinate (INFERENCE on maturity); 1.x API; MIT
limitations: 'PgQueuer does not automatically prune pgqueuer_log' - periodic deletes or partitioning required.
Entrypoints must be `async def`; sync code needs threads (INFERENCE).
At-least-once delivery: job functions must be idempotent or checkpoint progress (stated in reliability doc).
Single primary maintainer (INFERENCE from repository metadata); bus-factor risk for a core infrastructure dependency.

evidence.claim: LISTEN/NOTIFY wake-up with polling fallback; FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED claims; asyncpg and psycopg drivers; transactional enqueue; per-entrypoint concurrency limits; cron-style recurring tasks and execute_after; custom executors for retry/backoff; Prometheus metrics, tracing, dashboard; in-memory test mode; MIT; Python 3.11+, PostgreSQL 12+
PyPI v1.3.2 released 2026-07-27; Python >=3.10; MIT; optional Logfire/Sentry/OpenTelemetry integrations; `pgq install`

Retries: raise RetryRequested(delay, reason); DatabaseRetryEntrypointExecutor with max_attempts and initial_delay exponential backoff; heartbeat_timeout makes stalled 'picked' jobs re-pickable; dedupe_key enforced by 'UNIQUE (dedupe_key) WHERE status IN (queued, picked)'; on_conflict='skip'; pgqueuer_log and pgqueuer_statistics (log_aggregation_interval); log not auto-pruned; at-least-once

Entrypoints via @pgq.entrypoint() with concurrency_limit, on_failure ('delete'/'hold'), accepts_context; QueueManager dequeues batches with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; SchedulerManager uses FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED 'to ensure only one worker runs each scheduled task, even across multiple processes'; Queries.requeue_jobs()

providers.relevance_to_cascade_oracle: Runner-up to Procrastinate. It wins on built-in observability (Prometheus, tracing, dashboard), automatic stalled-job re-pickup, and first-class dedupe_key; it loses on ecosystem maturity and sync support. Keep task bodies as plain functions so a switch is cheap if Procrastinate's ops gaps (dashboard, auto-stall recovery) prove costly.

providers.name: Broker-backed queues and in-process schedulers: Celery, Dramatiq, arq, APScheduler (not recommended as primary)
providers.authority: Celery project; Bogdan Popa (Dramatiq); Samuel Colvin (arq); Alex Grönholm (APScheduler)

access.mechanism: PyPI packages; Celery/Dramatiq/arq require an external broker (RabbitMQ/Redis); APScheduler runs inside a Python process

providers.temporal_resolution: Cron-style scheduling via celery beat, APScheduler triggers, arq cron jobs
providers.quality_flags: Celery and Dramatiq mature; arq 'maintained in a limited capacity only'; APScheduler 4.x explicitly not production-ready
providers.licensing: Celery BSD-3-Clause; Dramatiq LGPL-3.0-or-later; arq MIT; APScheduler MIT
limitations: Celery has no PostgreSQL broker: stable brokers are RabbitMQ, Redis, Amazon SQS (Zookeeper/Kafka/GCP Pub/Sub experimental); SQLAlchemy is only a result backend. Violates the 'Postgres as the only infra' constraint.
Celery beat: 'You have to ensure only a single scheduler is running for a schedule at a time, otherwise you'd end up with duplicate tasks' - HA scheduling needs external coordination.

Dramatiq: brokers are RabbitMQ and Redis; 'APScheduler is the recommended scheduler to use with Dramatiq' (no built-in cron); async actors run on a single event-loop thread per worker process with concurrency still bounded by worker threads (8 default).

arq: Redis only; 'pessimistic execution' (jobs rerun after crash, favours multiple times over zero times - so idempotency is mandatory); PyPI description says it is 'maintained in a limited capacity only'.

APScheduler 3.x is an in-process scheduler without multi-node job-store coordination (INFERENCE for 3.x; 4.x adds shareable data stores and lease extension but 'The v4.0 series is provided as a pre-release and may change in a backwards incompatible fashion without any migration pathway, so do NOT use this release in production!').

evidence.claim: Celery brokers: RabbitMQ/Redis/SQS stable; Zookeeper/Kafka/Pub/Sub experimental; no PostgreSQL broker; 'SQLAlchemy is a backend'; docs for 5.6.3
